paragraphs: One-sentence judgment | this occupation is worth further verification only if you are willing to independently take on a patient's diagnosis, treatment, and follow-up in outpatient or inpatient settings, can maintain assessment and communication under high-intensity and high-precision demands, and accept the continuing requirements of graduate nursing education, state licensure, and national certification; being drawn to the idea of being able to prescribe or having higher status is not enough by itself.

Core output | linking history and physical examination, diagnosis and differential, treatment and medication plans, test result interpretation, and patient education and follow-up arrangements into a traceable care record: reviewable clinical decisions and care records, not a conclusion from one consultation.

20—120 minute safe trial | use a fictional case for one off-site exercise: based on the given chief complaint, vital signs, and past history excerpts, write out three differential diagnoses that need priority consideration and two examinations that must be arranged immediately, and write out a management outline including medication verification and a follow-up plan. The exercise uses only fictional data, and no examination, diagnosis, prescription, or procedure may be performed on any real patient.

First threshold | confirm the authority and authorization boundary first: who may diagnose, order tests, prescribe, and adjust plans. This occupation in the United States requires being a registered nurse with graduate education and obtaining state licensure and national certification before practicing within state law and institutional authorization; nurses in mainland China execute physician orders in accordance with law and do not have independent diagnostic and prescribing authority (the National Health Commission's 2024 reply made clear that granting nurses prescribing authority still lacks a legal and regulatory basis).

entries: Diagnosis and prescribing | diagnose and treat acute, episodic, or chronic illness independently or collaboratively, and order tests and medications within the scope of state regulations and institutional authorization.

History and physical examination | collect and record history, symptoms, and physical examination findings, and perform routine or annual physical examinations and primary care procedures (suturing, splinting, immunizations, sampling, debridement, and so on).

Test interpretation | order, perform, or interpret diagnostic tests such as laboratory work and imaging (such as complete blood counts, electrocardiograms, and X-rays), and use them to determine the next step.
Health management and education | guide patients in self-managing acute and chronic illness and provide information on health promotion, risk factor reduction, and disease prevention.

Medication safety | determine medication dosage, route, and frequency according to characteristics such as age and sex, monitor and respond to adverse drug reactions, and pay attention to vulnerable groups such as infants, pregnant and postpartum women, and older adults.
Referral and collaboration | refer cases beyond the scope of practice to specialists, and collaborate with other healthcare providers on complex, unstable, comorbid, or emergency situations.
Records and coordination | maintain complete and detailed patient medical care plans and prognosis records, and supervise or coordinate the work of patient care and support staff.

paragraphs: Nurse Practitioners (O*NET-SOC 29-1171.00, Nurse Practitioners) diagnose and treat acute, episodic, or chronic illness independently or as a member of a healthcare team, with a focus on health promotion and disease prevention; they may order, perform, or interpret diagnostic tests such as laboratory work and X-rays and may prescribe medications; this occupation in the United States requires a registered nurse with professional graduate education. The work includes: developing treatment plans based on scientific principles, nursing standards, and professional practice guidelines; analyzing and interpreting history, symptoms, physical examination findings, or diagnostic information to make a diagnosis; prescribing medication dosage, route, and frequency; diagnosing or treating chronic and acute health problems (such as hypertension, diabetes, infections, and injuries); detecting and responding to adverse drug reactions; guiding patients in self-managing illness; performing primary care procedures; referring cases beyond the scope of practice; and recording care plans and prognosis in the medical record.

The work settings are mainly hospitals, physicians' offices, and outpatient clinics: O*NET shows 91% have a regular work schedule and 52% work more than 40 hours per week; 83% have a lot of decision freedom, 74% make decisions daily that affect the results of others or the organization, and 57% consider the decision results very important; 80% consider cooperation with others (the work team) extremely important. Most advanced practice registered nurses work full time.

Exposure and precision requirements concentrate in clinical contact: O*NET shows 87% exposed to disease or infection daily, 65% wear common protective or safety equipment daily, 74% consider precision or accuracy extremely important, 70% consider the consequences of error extremely serious, and 43% report very high responsibility for the health and safety of others; 39% encounter conflict situations at least weekly, and 48% face strict deadlines daily.

The O*NET interest code is ISC (Investigative, Social, Conventional); work styles are mainly sincerity, adaptability, persistence, empathy, stress tolerance, self-control, social orientation, achievement orientation, cooperation, and inquisitiveness; Job Zone 5 (SVP 8.0 and above), and the education survey shows 65% master's degrees, 26% doctoral degrees, and 4% bachelor's degrees. These dimensions describe activity preferences and work requirements and cannot be treated as hiring standards, ability assessment conclusions, or career destiny judgments.

The capability focus is mapping symptoms, signs, and test results to care decisions and stating the basis: being able to map history and physical examination findings to possible diagnoses, and stating the criteria for continued observation, further examination, or immediate handling or referral; the ability list is mainly active listening, critical thinking, reading comprehension, active learning, monitoring, speaking, and writing.

Responsibility boundary (United States) | nurse practitioners are advanced practice registered nurses who may diagnose, order tests, and prescribe within state law and institutional authorization, and manage patients independently or collaboratively; the scope of practice varies by state (full, restricted, or transition to practice), and a state registered nurse license, completed graduate education, and a passed national certification examination are required.

Responsibility boundary (mainland China) | mainland China has no independent practice and prescribing occupation corresponding one-to-one with O*NET 29-1171.00. Nurse practice requires obtaining a Nurse Practice Certificate through practice registration (valid for 5 years), executing physician orders in accordance with law, and providing health education and specialty nursing; the National Health Commission's 2024 reply made clear that granting nurses prescribing authority currently still lacks a legal and regulatory basis, and position duties are determined by institutional rules and competent department provisions.

Nurse practitioners are adjacent to nurse anesthetists, nurse midwives, physician assistants, registered nurses, and specialty nursing directions, and should be distinguished by the main work object, independent practice authority, and prescribing and referral boundaries rather than by similarity of job titles.

The comparison objects in this table come from the official tasks of O*NET 29-1171.00 and the official occupation descriptions and current systems of adjacent occupations; this occupation in the United States is a role among advanced practice registered nurses focused on primary and specialty care, requires graduate education and state licensure and national certification, and its scope of practice varies by state.

The table below compares this occupation with adjacent directions on the same dimensions: main work object, core output, key differences, and selection signals; the comparison is for career exploration and does not represent mutual qualification recognition, automatic transfer, or a hiring promise.

Physician assistants work under physician supervision or collaboration and may prescribe in most states; nurse anesthetists focus on anesthesia and perioperative management; nurse midwives focus on continuity of maternity care; registered nurses focus on nursing assessment and carrying out orders and usually do not hold independent diagnostic and prescribing authority. The core difference of this occupation is that it is an advanced practice care role grounded in nursing, diagnosing and prescribing independently within the authorized scope.

If you want to take on fuller diagnostic, treatment, and prescribing responsibility on a nursing foundation and are willing to complete graduate education and national certification, you may continue verifying this occupation; if you would rather focus on anesthesia, maternity, or surgical support, you should choose the nurse anesthetist, nurse midwife, or physician assistant path respectively and check each one's state authorization and supervision requirements.

paragraphs: The key signals of fit for this occupation are: being able to maintain assessment and recording habits under high-precision demands, being able to communicate effectively with patients and families, being able to re-check and refer promptly when uncertain, and being willing to take on continuing education and certification requirements; interest and work style labels cannot determine fit.

Interest codes and work styles come from the O*NET 29-1171.00 summary and are exploratory evidence; the fit signals and trial design on this page are editorial synthesis and do not constitute selection standards, ability assessment, or a hiring promise.

Boundary statement | this list cannot replace the institution's diagnostic and treatment standards, prescription and medication management systems, infection control systems, or adverse event reporting systems. The main risks center on: missed diagnosis and differential, delayed test result interpretation, prescribing and medication errors, inadequate adverse drug reaction monitoring, infection and body fluid exposure, and missing records and follow-up; control requirements should be tailored to institutional authorization and state law.

Direct answer | the main risks of this occupation are diagnostic error or delay, misinterpretation of tests, prescription dosage and interaction errors, failure to promptly identify adverse drug reactions, inadequate procedural and nosocomial infection control, and missing records and follow-up; control depends on structured interviews and physical examinations, diagnostic and medication verification processes, test result re-checking, referral channels, and post-exposure handling systems.

Evidence scope | the risk items come from the tasks and work context of O*NET 29-1171.00 (87% exposed to disease or infection daily, 74% consider precision extremely important, 70% consider the consequences of error extremely serious, 43% report very high responsibility for the health and safety of others, 48% face time pressure daily, and 39% encounter conflict situations more than weekly), and from the provisions of China's Nurses Regulation on critical condition reporting and occupational health surveillance; control requirements should be tailored to the institution and local rules.

Nurse practitioners and the physician, pharmacist, and nursing team are affected; no newcomer or high-load outpatient group comparison data was obtained this round, and it is not asserted that they are most likely to omit steps.

Possible consequences | diagnostic or interpretation delays may affect treatment effect and patient safety; prescription or medication errors cause direct harm; unidentified adverse drug reactions delay handling; inadequate infection exposure protection affects occupational health; and missing records and follow-up affect care continuity and responsibility traceability.

Editorial example of position requirements, not an open announcement. U.S. requirements are an RN, accredited NP graduate education, matching certification, state NP / APRN and prescribing authority, and institutional authorization; AANP does not award certification, AANPCB operates under the NPCB brand, and ANCC and others are chosen by direction. Capability progression should start with supervised learning of interviews, physical examinations, and common disease management, then after obtaining registered nurse licensure, graduate education, and national certification take on independent or collaborative care according to state authorization, then participate in complex comorbidity and chronic disease management, and finally enter mentoring, quality improvement, and guideline development; each step is premised on license, certification, state law authorization scope, and institutional position authorization.

Readiness evidence should include: structured interview and physical examination records, diagnostic and differential basis, prescription and medication verification records, test interpretation records, patient education and follow-up records, and simulated case exercise records; these materials are used to show decision and recording habits and do not represent real clinical qualification.

Qualification boundary (United States): nurse practitioners must hold a state registered nurse license, complete accredited graduate education, and pass a national certification examination; the scope of independent practice and prescribing varies by state (full, restricted, or transition to practice) and is governed by state law and institutional authorization.

Works and exercise materials should use fictional patient data and write out the input, basis for judgment, management, and reviewer; real patient information must not be used, and paper exercises must not be treated as proof of real care authorization.

Record requirements: anything entering the formal medical record must be traceable, keeping the original data, basis for judgment, and signature; tool-generated summaries must be manually re-checked before entering the record.

Next step suggestion: first check the target state or institution's license, certification, and scope of practice requirements, then complete this page's works list with simulated cases, and finally verify fit through comparative feedback with nurse practitioners or incumbent staff.

subject.name: Nurse Practitioners
subject.summary: Nurse Practitioners (O*NET-SOC 29-1171.00, Nurse Practitioners) diagnose and treat acute, episodic, or chronic illness independently or as a member of a healthcare team, with a focus on health promotion and disease prevention; they may order, perform, or interpret diagnostic tests such as laboratory work and imaging and may prescribe medications. This occupation in the United States requires a registered nurse with professional graduate education. This page uses only official sources to explain the occupational scope, tasks, China-U.S. admission differences, and statistical scope.
